title: S*LM
lines: S*LM presents intelligence as a division of cognitive labor among different computational roles.
The star includes small, specialized, and symbolic components, without treating them as interchangeable.
Some tasks need broad interpretation, while others require exact execution or local operation.
The book asks how much generality each role actually needs.
Readers can evaluate a research programme about allocation, rather than another promise of universal replacement.

title: Roles have different obligations
lines: Interpreting an ambiguous request and executing an exact calculation are different computational jobs.
A role may need broad knowledge, while another needs a tightly constrained output.
The book separates these requirements before choosing a model or symbolic engine.
Contracts and authority matter because combining competent components can still produce an unreliable system.
The proposed unit of design is therefore the complete allocation of work.

title: Specialization must earn its cost
lines: Repeated work may justify a compact policy, deterministic procedure, or specialized model.
That possibility depends on maintenance, changing tasks, verification, and end-to-end performance.
A cheaper component is not a saving if the surrounding workflow becomes unreliable.
The book states hypotheses and conditions that could weaken its proposed approach.
It keeps access to general models and human judgment where narrower components remain insufficient.

title: Read for sufficient generality
lines: Begin with the taxonomy separating size, specialization, and symbolic structure.
Then follow the language stack from interpretation through action, verification, and recovery.
The research programme asks how role requirements can guide choices across different workflows.
S*LM offers a way to evaluate heterogeneous systems without assuming specialization always wins.
Read it to decide where general intelligence is needed, and where a narrower obligation is clearer.
